inline.s: These two kinds of dharma can be practiced side by side without conflict. Freedom from marks is itself freedom from thought, and only freedom from thought makes freedom from marks possible; hence it is said that they do not conflict. Yet freedom from marks removes only the coarser layer of deluded thought, the kind that arises in pursuit of illusory marks; freedom from thought removes the subtler layer, the kind from which illusory marks arise along with thought. Hence both must be practiced together. Practicing them together does not mean being rigidly bound to freedom from marks first and freedom from thought afterward. It means that when one is free from marks one also cultivates freedom from thought, so that freedom from marks can become complete; and that when one is free from thought one also cultivates freedom from marks, so that freedom from thought gains further skillful means. They should be practiced simultaneously, side by side.

In short, because sentient beings are deluded by all marks of dharma, they never know to turn back and illumine their own nature. How should they know that their own nature is of one substance with sentient beings? How should they know that the five aggregates and six faculties within, and all dharmas such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth without, are all made by mind alone? Not knowing this, they do not know that the Buddha's teaching that one should not dwell in any dharma is meant to rid them of the fault of discrimination, attachment, and grasping at marks, and has nothing whatever to do with the dharmas themselves. Once the fault of grasping at marks is removed, then the five aggregates within and all dharmas such as mountains and rivers without are, as the Surangama Sutra says, all the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind, the pure and luminous essence of nature. Why? Because all dharmas have only marks and no nature of their own. It is not that they have no nature: the nature of all dharmas is the self-nature itself. Why? Because there is one true dharma-realm. How then could they be dismissed? Why should they be dismissed? This is the true meaning of every dharma being thus. Hence the Awakening of Faith says: "This essence of true suchness has nothing that can be dismissed, because all dharmas are wholly real. Nor is there anything that can be established, because all dharmas are wholly such." You should know that anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is simply another name for true suchness. To dwell in it is still to grasp at marks. Where there is something grasped, there is something established. Though you dismiss every mark of dharma, if you set up the mark of bodhi alone, then it is no longer the case that all dharmas are such. Why? Because where there is establishment there is rejection. The self-nature is the source of all dharmas, excluding nothing, lacking nothing. To establish one and reject the rest is not the whole nature. How could that be the unexcelled and perfectly equal, how could it be true enlightenment?

In the first half of this sutra, the dismissing of every mark of dharma in order to reveal bodhi serves only to remove the fault of grasping at all dharmas. Lest one should still grasp at bodhi itself, the second half opens its first chapter by dismissing that as well. Once this fault is dismissed, the virtue of the nature is completely manifested, and every dharma is thus. There is nothing to dismiss, and nothing to establish. This is the final goal of the practitioner. All the meanings taught since the sutra began also come to rest here. Therefore the section on every dharma being thus is a vital meaning in the whole sutra, and indeed a vital meaning in all Mahayana Buddhadharma. Everything said afterward is nothing but an unfolding and a confirmation of this meaning. Nor is there anything in the first half that does not incline toward this meaning and gather it in. Here the World-Honored One lays out his own personal realization completely, without holding anything back, and teaches it in full detail, so that sentient beings may awaken through it and enter through it.

Therefore, for every dharma to be thus, every emotional clinging must be utterly dismissed; only realization knows it, and it cannot be put into empty words. If one has not dismissed the fault of grasping in the slightest, and yet tells others that everything is thus, then every dharma becomes an obstruction; how could every dharma be thus? Such a one is simply a deluded person. To speak wildly of prajñā is an offense that leads to falling into the uninterrupted hell, because such a one misleads and confuses sentient beings, causing them to slander the Buddha and the Dharma and to belittle the Three Jewels. You should know that if one has truly realized every dharma being thus, one will certainly be able to act it out: compressing immeasurable kalpas into a single moment, extending a single moment into immeasurable kalpas, fitting Mount Sumeru into a mustard seed, transforming the saha world into a Pure Land. Only at this stage, where all phenomena are without obstruction, may such words be spoken. All students should simply contemplate every dharma as thus, so as to dismiss utterly the clinging of self-view and pervasive discrimination, and thereby seek to enter realization. That is what is fitting. How could one give rise to great pride and lightly turn the words "all is thus" into a mere topic of talk? Consider the very end of this sutra, which is also the beginning of the circulation section: after speaking of thus, thus, and unmoved, it immediately continues, "Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; like dew, and like lightning; they should be contemplated thus." This precisely shows that thus, thus, and unmoved must be entered through contemplating all dharmas as dreamlike and illusory. To contemplate them as dream, illusion, and the rest is to dismiss emotional clinging. These are the crucial points in the sutra, and they must not be neglected.

What does it mean that the meaning of the first half is gathered in here? Let me explain briefly, to open the gate of awakening. For example: "If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathagata." Consider: if one sees that marks are precisely no marks, is that not every dharma being thus? Hence it says, "then you see the Tathagata." Whenever the sutra says that such-and-such is not such-and-such, it is pointing to this meaning. Again: "When the mind of faith is pure, the real mark is produced." You should know that it is because there is no discrimination or attachment that the mind afterward becomes pure; when the mind is pure, the real mark is produced. The real mark means no mark and no non-mark, and then every dharma is thus. Hence it says: one should produce a pure mind; one should produce the mind while not dwelling; one should produce the mind that does not dwell; one should, free from all marks, arouse the bodhi mind and practice the six paramitas; if the mind dwells, then it does not dwell rightly. Again: one should not grasp dharmas, and should not grasp non-dharmas. Not grasping dharmas is because all dharmas are thus and nothing can be established. Not grasping non-dharmas is because all dharmas are real and nothing can be dismissed. This is exactly what is meant by every dharma being thus. Because every dharma is thus, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathagata can teach. Therefore dharma and non-dharma are both negated; both cannot be grasped and both cannot be spoken. That all sages and worthies differ only through the unconditioned dharma is because, since every dharma is thus, every dharma is real. (This is why the Lotus Sutra says, "This dharma abides in the station of dharma; the marks of the world are ever abiding.") Hence all dharmas are pure by nature and are in no way fabricated; therefore they are called unconditioned. All sages and worthies without exception cultivate and realize this. But because the depth of their practice differs, there are differences in becoming worthies and becoming sages. In truth, in the dharma of oneness, how could there ever have been any difference? Other points may be thought through by this standard.

In short, if one comprehends that every dharma is thus, and harmonizes with it, then there is no such thing as emptiness, no such thing as existence, and no such thing as the middle; and then emptiness is no obstacle, existence is no obstacle, and there is neither emptiness nor the provisional that is not the middle. Why? Once the fault of self-view and emotional clinging has been utterly dismissed, then to see marks is to see the nature; everything is the Way, and nothing is unacceptable. Hence the sutras such as the Most Victorious King and the Vimalakirti say: the five aggregates are the dharma-body; birth and death are nirvana; affliction is bodhi. All of them reveal the meaning that every dharma is thus. If even a little discrimination and attachment remains unbroken, then wherever one turns one is blocked; nothing is the Way, and nothing is acceptable. Even if one clings to nothing else but still clings to one bodhi, that too is grasping at marks and discrimination, and one obstructs one's own substance of enlightenment. Then what is called the middle is not the middle, to say nothing of clinging to existence or inclining to emptiness. For all who arouse the mind to save themselves and others, hoping to illumine the nature and see the Buddha, the essential method lies wholly here. What is that method? According to the teaching of this sutra, it is freedom from marks and freedom from thought. You should know that since this sutra is the source from which all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth, whatever it teaches is nothing but root meaning and ultimate meaning. The other thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises all manifest and support this meaning. Therefore I have now set out this vital meaning in full detail, thoroughly and completely, and all good teachers should ponder it well.

(Zi) Second, explaining that every dharma is thus. In four: (Chou) First, the Thus in respect of name; second, the Thus in respect of the fruit of virtue; third, the Thus in respect of all dharmas; fourth, the Thus in respect of the reward body.
(Chou) First, the Thus in respect of name.
"Why? Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas."

The line "Why?" is the Buddha's own posing of a question. He asks: of the text above, which says that only where there is no bodhi dharma can one be granted the prediction of Buddhahood, and only where there is no bodhi dharma can the Tathagata attain bodhi, what is the reason? After "Tathagata," he poses his own answer. It is as if he said: the Buddha is called Tathagata; do you also know the meaning of Tathagata? Its meaning is nothing else: it is precisely because he is free from the empty marks of all dharmas' differences and has realized the true nature of the oneness of all dharmas. You should know that the Buddha does not see the marks of difference among dharmas; this is what is meant by "thus." Nor does the Buddha see the mark of any single dharma being different; this is what is meant by "the suchness of all dharmas." Thus means the meaning of no difference, and also the meaning of no distinctness: it says that the nature of dharma has no divergence. That the nature of dharma has no divergence is because it is empty and still. Hence "the suchness of all dharmas" is the meaning that the nature of dharma is empty and still. One is named Tathagata because one has realized the nature that is empty and still. If one were to hold that there is an emptiness and stillness, that would already be divergence, and it would not be empty and still; how could one be called Tathagata? Hence it is said: Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. (Stress the word thus.) How then could one who arouses the unexcelled, perfectly equal enlightenment keep in mind the mark of having aroused that enlightenment, so that it is not empty and still?

Again, the sutra speaks of "all dharmas," which is not-one; and it further speaks of "thus," which is not-distinct. Not-one and not-distinct: such is the nature of dharma. The Buddha is called the Greatly Awakened One because he has ultimately awakened to this nature of dharma that is not-one and not-distinct. Hence it is said: Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. (Stress both all dharmas and thus.) You should know that because it is not-one, the dharma of bodhi should not be grasped; and because it is not-distinct, the dharma of bodhi should likewise not be grasped. (The first statement treats essence alone; the second treats essence together with mark and function.) Seen in this light, to assert firmly that all dharmas are all dharmas is wrong, for they are one thus even though they are many; (stress oneness-thus) and to assert firmly that all dharmas are not all dharmas is also wrong, for they are the oneness-thus of all dharmas. (Stress all dharmas.)

The crux of all this depends entirely on whether one clings or not. If one does not cling to existence, all dharmas do not obstruct the oneness-thus; if one does not cling to emptiness, the oneness-thus does not obstruct all dharmas. To cling to all dharmas is not thus; to cling to the Thus is not the suchness of all dharmas. Hence whatever the Tathagata teaches can neither be grasped nor spoken. It cannot be grasped because the nature of all dharmas is the one true suchness, without discrimination, and because it is the equality of differences. It cannot be spoken because the nature of true suchness is not apart from all dharmas and is known only through realization, and because within difference one sees equality. Therefore one who has awakened should be free from all marks and cultivate the six paramitas and myriad practices. Being free from all marks is because on the ground of ultimate reality one does not stain a single mote of dust; cultivating myriad practices is because within the gate of Buddha-work one does not abandon a single dharma. Because all dharmas are one thus, one should not abandon a single dharma; because it is the dharma of oneness-thus, one should not stain a single mote of dust. To awaken thus, to be free thus, to cultivate thus, is for dharma to accord and nature to accord, and so to attain accord in realization.

In short, to be blind to equality and grasp at difference is for the mind to turn along with dharmas, so that even non-dharmas become obstructions. To see equality within difference is for dharmas to turn along with the mind, so that no dharma is anything but true suchness. What the ancient worthies called greeting guests and seeing them off, carrying water and hauling firewood, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, so that at every hour of the day, whatever dharma one picks up is it, is a fine picture of the man of no affairs enjoying himself. You should know that the world is originally without affairs; it is ordinary people who trouble themselves. In the midst of no emptiness and no existence, they grasp at marks of emptiness and existence. In the midst of no good and no evil, they think of good and think of evil. Deluded marks fly about in confusion; is this not troubling oneself? How free it is to pick something up and find it is it! The ancient worthies also said: before awakening, mountains are mountains and waters are waters. After awakening, mountains are not mountains and waters are not waters. When mountains are mountains and waters are waters, one sees only all dharmas. When mountains are not mountains and waters are not waters, one sees only the oneness-thus. And there is a song of awakening that says: the blue mountains are still the same blue mountains. It means that all dharmas remain as they were, yet in seeing the oneness-thus of all dharmas, though the blue mountains are the same as before, their whole aspect is brilliantly new.

"Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas" appears to explain only the word thus, but in fact the word come is explained within it as well. How is this so? There is coming and there is going: these are marks of difference, that is, the oneness of all dharmas. Since all dharmas are thus, coming is thus too. All sentient beings come but are not thus. The sages of the Two Vehicles are thus but do not come. Bodhisattvas at the provisional stages are thus but not yet wholly thus, and though they come, they cannot come everywhere. Only the Buddha, the Tathagata, having realized the oneness of nature, comes everywhere to the very limit of true suchness. True suchness has no limit, so his coming has no limit. True suchness is unmoved, so his coming is unmoved. Though he is named as coming, in truth he comes without a mark of coming, and comes without coming. You should know that he is named Tathagata to make clear that his coming has no mark of coming, hence "thus"; and to make clear that his thus has no mark of thus, hence "come." (The meaning of this passage is that when we speak in terms of the marks of coming and going, the two words all dharmas cover it; when we speak of coming without a mark of coming, the word thus covers it. It also makes clear the suchness of all dharmas: by means of all dharmas one dismisses the Thus, and by means of the Thus one dismisses all dharmas, revealing the virtue of nature in which negation and illumination are simultaneous. All that has been said above is this meaning. The words quoted from the ancient worthies are not idle talk. Look into this.)
(Chou) Second, the Thus in respect of the fruit of virtue. In two: (Yin) First, explaining that there is no dharma; second, explaining the oneness-thus.
(Yin) First, explaining that there is no dharma.
"If someone says that the Tathagata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Subhuti, in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"If someone" means "perhaps someone." Since the text above contains the words "the Tathagata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," the Buddha fears that one who does not grasp the meaning, hearing that Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas, may accordingly doubt: since the meaning of Tathagata is the oneness of all dharmas, then it is clear that there is no bodhi to be attained. Why then did he say above that the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? To block this doubt, he sets up a hypothetical saying and again calls the elder and tells him: what this person says arises from suspecting that there is still a dharma. He does not realize that in truth there is no dharma. It is only to make clear that his enlightenment is already ultimate, and that there is no way to name it, so it is named the Buddha's attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Implied in these words is that, spoken in terms of the virtue of nature, it truly is the oneness of all dharmas. Hence here he does not say Tathagata but says Buddha, precisely to make clear that the one who is called the attainer of bodhi is so called to show that he has already realized unexcelled, perfectly equal enlightenment, which is the fruit of the oneness of all dharmas. How could it mean that there is a bodhi dharma to be attained? What doubt is there? The text below further uses the meaning of neither real nor unreal to make clear that he is said to attain while in truth attaining nothing, and that although nothing is attained it may still be called attainment. Then it will be all the clearer.
(Yin) Second, explaining the oneness-thus.
"Subhuti, in the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata has attained, therein there is neither the real nor the unreal."

"Therein" means within what is attained. The meaning is: even granting what that person says, that the Tathagata attains bodhi, he does not realize that what the Tathagata attains is nothing but neither real nor unreal. Neither real nor unreal is precisely the suchness of all dharmas. This meaning should be expounded at length so that it may be grasped.

(1) This resembles the words above, "The dharma that the Tathagata has attained, this dharma is neither real nor unreal," yet the meaning is very different. The passage above explains that the dharma is real. It says that the dharma the Tathagata has attained is the real mark. The real mark is no mark and no non-mark. No mark is no reality; no non-mark is no unreality. To speak ultimately, the real mark has neither mark nor non-mark, hence it is said to be neither real nor unreal, meaning that both reality and unreality are absent. This is the real dharma, and it confirms the statement above about the real.

Here the text explains that in truth there is no dharma. Since there is already no dharma, how much less is there anything attained? Granting the words of that person, we may say that the Tathagata attains; yet if we look into it, therein nothing whatever is attained. Why? Because in truth there is no dharma. It is only a provisional name for attainment, and is not real. Yet there is no harm in saying that the Tathagata attains. Why? Because what is attained is nothing but thus; attaining this is what makes one called Tathagata. It is not unreal. (This is directed at the explanation above.)

(2) Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is another name for the awakened nature of true suchness. Since Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas, it is as much as to say that one is called Tathagata because one has realized the awakened nature of true suchness. This is enough to prove that what the Tathagata attains is nothing but the oneness-thus. Hence although it is named attainment, within that attainment there is nothing real, because the awakened nature is empty and still; and there is nothing unreal, because the awakened nature is perfectly manifest. Hence it is said: therein there is neither the real nor the unreal. In short, there is no such thing as an attainment that has an attainment; this is no reality. It is not that there is no such thing as an attainment that has no attainment; this is no unreality. This is exactly what the Madhyamaka-sastra means by: "Where there is no grasping subject or object, there is existence; where there is a grasping subject or object, there is not." It is also what the Buddha-nature Treatise says: "Because the adventitious dust is empty, it is apart from the dharma-realm. Because the supreme dharma is not empty, it follows the dharma-realm." The adventitious dust being empty, therefore no reality; the supreme dharma not being empty, therefore no unreality. You should know that the Buddha says this to make clear that one must not hear of attainment and suspect that there is a dharma, and must not hear that there is no dharma and suspect that there is ultimately no realization. (This explains the meaning in terms of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.)

(3) To speak of no reality is to make clear that it illumines while ever still. To speak of no unreality is to make clear that it is still while ever illumining. Neither real nor unreal is precisely double negation and double illumination, stillness and illumination simultaneous. Therein not a single dharma arises, because it is still. Yet not a single dharma fails to appear, because it illumines. Not a single dharma arises: in truth there is no dharma, hence no reality. Not a single dharma fails to appear: all dharmas are one thus, hence no unreality. This is what is meant by anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. That the Tathagata attains means that he attains this. (This explains the meaning in terms of stillness and illumination simultaneous.)

(4) Neither real nor unreal is the Awakening of Faith's meaning of "empty in accordance with reality" and "not empty in accordance with reality." In accordance with reality is true suchness, and because true suchness is the real essence of nature it is called in accordance with reality. It makes clear that all dharmas are one thus, and this is the real. The treatise explains the meaning of empty in accordance with reality: "What is called empty is that from the very beginning all defiled dharmas do not correspond. That is to say, it is free from the marks of difference of all dharmas, because there is no deluded mind or thought." This says that although the minds of all sentient beings contain deluded thoughts and all the defiled and impure marks of difference arising from subject and object in opposition, this essence of the nature in accordance with reality still remains ever constant and unchanging, because from the very beginning the one purity and the one defilement do not correspond. Not corresponding means being apart. How are they apart? Because from the very beginning the essence in accordance with reality is itself not deluded mind or thought. It also says: "You should know that the self-nature of true suchness is neither with marks nor without marks, and indeed neither one nor different, nor both. In sum, because there is deluded mind, moment by moment discriminating, none of it corresponds; therefore it is called empty. If one is apart from deluded mind, in truth there is nothing to be emptied." This says that what is called empty is the emptying of deluded thoughts and marks of difference. Hence it says neither with marks nor without marks, and indeed neither one nor different, nor both. The meaning is that one is free from marks. If one is utterly free from all the four propositions of opposition, such as existence, non-existence, oneness, and difference, then one is apart from deluded mind and thought. Once these are apart, the self-nature of true suchness appears. Hence it says: if one is apart from deluded mind, in truth there is nothing to be emptied. This makes clear that what is called empty does not mean the absence of the self-nature of true suchness. How then can deluded mind and thought be separated from and emptied? Because all the deluded mind of moment-by-moment discrimination does not by nature correspond with the self-nature of true suchness. This makes clear that the self-nature is itself empty, and so can be emptied. Yet once deluded thoughts and defiled marks are empty, true suchness appears. This further makes clear that it is empty yet not empty.

It explains the meaning of not empty in accordance with reality: "What is called not empty is that, since it has already revealed that the essence of dharma is empty and without delusion, it is the true mind, ever constant and unchanging, fulfilled in pure dharmas; therefore it is called not empty." This says that once the essence of dharma is empty of all deluded thoughts, it is the true mind, ever constant and unchanging, fulfilled in immeasurable pure dharmas of virtue; hence not empty. The essence of dharma means the true nature of the oneness-thus, which is called true suchness. True suchness is the essence of all dharmas, hence it is called the essence of dharma. The treatise also says: "Nor are there any marks to be grasped, because the realm beyond thought is only corresponded with through realization." This says that the true nature of the oneness of all dharmas, which is the essence of all dharmas, is in truth without dharma and should not be dwelt in, because it is a realm beyond thought, known only through realization. Hence it says that there are also no marks to be grasped, making clear that it is not empty yet empty.

Considering the meanings of the treatise as set out above: empty in accordance with reality is no reality; not empty in accordance with reality is no unreality. Empty yet not empty: no reality is likewise no unreality. Not empty yet empty: no unreality is likewise no reality. This is the true essence of all dharmas, thus and unmoved. Hence here the Buddha says that in the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata has attained, therein there is neither the real nor the unreal. This is precisely explaining the passage above, that Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. Moreover, if one reads the treatise carefully, it plainly says that not empty comes from empty, and one may know that no unreality comes from no reality, and that the oneness of all dharmas comes from there being in truth no dharma. Using the treatise to prove the sutra, the meaning is perfectly clear. One may also see that the two passages quoted from the treatise are no different from a fusion of the main purport of this sutra. Hence one who would understand this sutra cannot but read the Awakening of Faith. (This explains the meaning by way of the Awakening of Faith.)

(5) No reality may be referred to all dharmas. All dharmas arise from conditions, hence no reality. No unreality may be referred to the Thus. True suchness is not empty, hence no unreality. The marks of all dharmas, though arisen from conditions, are without reality; the nature of all dharmas, however, is the same one true suchness and is without unreality. Hence it is said: therein there is neither the real nor the unreal, making clear that the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata has attained is in truth without dharma and without attainment, and is simply the realization of the suchness of all dharmas. (This explains the meaning by way of the suchness of all dharmas.)

(6) Neither real nor unreal is emptiness and existence as one thus, the virtue of nature as it inherently is. The Tathagata realizes this, and so teaches this section, causing sentient beings to awaken to it and cultivate it. You should know that these four words are perfectly equal and should not be seen as two separate halves, nor should they be rigidly divided into before and after. To view all dharmas as only real is to be an ordinary being; to view all dharmas as only unreal is to be of the Two Vehicles; and even to view all dharmas as unreal within the real and real within the unreal is still to be a bodhisattva at the provisional stages. Only the Buddha is not so: he views all dharmas as neither real nor unreal, as one whole. No reality is likewise no unreality; no unreality is likewise no reality. This is what is meant by the oneness of all dharmas, and it is also emptiness and existence simultaneous. One should awaken thus and cultivate thus. How does one cultivate? By producing a mind that dwells nowhere, and by being free from all marks while practicing giving and the six paramitas for the benefit of all sentient beings. One must make the time of being free from marks itself the time of benefiting, and the time of benefiting itself the time of being free from marks. This is to produce the non-dwelling mind; this is to arouse unexcelled bodhi. Then though it is called arousing, in truth there is no dharma of bodhi. In this way one may come to correspond with the awakened nature of neither real nor unreal, the oneness of all dharmas. Indeed, even such names and marks as neither real nor unreal and the oneness of all dharmas are themselves transcended. Only then is there no dharma, and only then can one correspond. If it were not so, then though one speaks of arousing bodhi, one has in fact already forgotten and lost bodhi. To forget and lose bodhi is to bring about demonic affairs. This is what we should constantly keep in mind. You should know that the World-Honored One tells of his own realization for no other reason than to make those who read the sutra and hear the Dharma practice according to the teaching. (This explains the meaning by way of urging cultivation.) Considering together all the meanings set out above, one may know that the Buddha's intent in teaching this section is simply to make clear that bodhi is without marks. Because it is without marks, there is no dharma by which to arouse bodhi and no dharma by which to attain bodhi; hence no reality. Because it is without marks, it is not that one dharma is bodhi, but that every dharma is bodhi; this is no unreality. Hence the next section is spoken, to complete this meaning. (This explains the meaning by way of introducing what follows.)
(Chou) Third, the Thus in respect of all dharmas. In two: (Yin) First, explaining that they are precisely all dharmas; second, explaining freedom from all marks.
(Yin) First, explaining that they are precisely all dharmas.
"Therefore the Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma."

Above it was said that Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. How is it seen that all dharmas are one thus? At this point it is summed up: because all dharmas are Buddhadharma. The words "therefore" connect most closely with neither real nor unreal, while tracing back to their source they connect with the suchness of all dharmas. The meaning is: because all dharmas arise from conditions and are therefore without reality, and because they are the same in accordance with reality and therefore without unreality, the Tathagata says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma. For from the suchness of all dharmas there opens out neither real nor unreal, and by means of neither real nor unreal it is made clear that all is so; and again by means of all being so, the oneness of all dharmas is confirmed. Generating one another, explaining one another, and completing one another in turn, they in fact all illuminate a single meaning. What single meaning? It is that one should dwell nowhere. This is why there is nothing in Buddhadharma that is not perfect, and nothing in the Buddha's teaching that is not wondrous.

The three words "the Tathagata says" are most important: they make clear that he speaks in terms of nature. If he spoke in terms of marks, all dharmas would be merely all dharmas; how could they be Buddhadharma? In sum, they make clear that when one is free from marks and contemplates the nature, everything is the Way. This is why the Surangama Sutra says that the five aggregates, the six entrances, and even the eighteen elements are all the wondrous true suchness of the Tathagatagarbha, and why the ancient worthies said that the yellow flowers outside the window are nothing but prajñā and the green bamboo before the courtyard is wholly true suchness. This is what is meant by all dharmas being Buddhadharma. In short, dharmas both worldly and world-transcending all arise from conditions. Knowing that they arise from conditions, and contemplating their undifferentiated nature and unchanging essence, then all is so and all dharmas are one thus. Otherwise, if one dwells in dharmas while arousing the mind and dwells in dharmas while practicing, then even Buddhadharma is not Buddhadharma, to say nothing of all dharmas. The Buddhadharma spoken of here should not be narrowly taken as the Dharma taught by the Buddha. Buddha means awakening; that all dharmas are dharmas of awakening means that every dharma is bodhi, making clear that bodhi is not some separate dharma. For when one is free from marks and contemplates the nature, one awakens and illumines the one true nature precisely upon all dharmas; hence every dharma is bodhi. This is spoken in terms of thus. To extend the point: whenever one practices worldly dharmas with compassion as the foundation, wholly for the sake of others and not for oneself, so that none of it conflicts with Buddhadharma, one may also say that worldly dharma is Buddhadharma. But if one's practice is nominally Buddhadharma while the mind seeks fame, gain, and respect, then Buddhadharma becomes worldly dharma. This section uses all dharmas to make clear the Thus; that is, it makes clear that all dharmas and Buddhadharma are one thus. It is precisely meant to dismiss the mark of the dharma of bodhi, because all dharmas are so. But if one mark of dharma is dismissed, all marks of dharma should be dismissed; hence the next section dismisses all dharmas as well.
(Yin) Second, explaining freedom from all marks.
"Subhuti, what are called all dharmas are not all dharmas; therefore they are called all dharmas."

This section dismisses all dharmas, and thereby confirms that they are all Buddhadharma. Why does it say that all dharmas are Buddhadharma? Because they are precisely not all dharmas. "Precisely not" is spoken in terms of nature. Spoken in terms of nature, it makes clear that one should not cling to marks; hence "precisely not." Knowing that they are precisely not, and so not clinging to marks, they are Buddhadharma and not all dharmas; hence it says that they are all Buddhadharma. Since they are all Buddhadharma, why does it again label and name them all dharmas? Because the provisional name of all dharmas is not absent; hence "are called." "Are called" is spoken in terms of marks. Spoken in terms of marks, its intent is to bring them back to nature; hence "are called." Knowing that it is a provisional name, one returns to nature, and though they are called all dharmas, they are all Buddhadharma; hence it says that all dharmas are Buddhadharma. For once one grasps that all dharmas are precisely not, one knows that they are merely provisional names; and once one grasps that all dharmas are called, one knows that they are not real. Then one no longer takes them as all dharmas but takes them as Buddhadharma. This is why all dharmas are Buddhadharma. You should know that "precisely not" and "are called," taken together, simply make clear the meaning of neither real nor unreal and of emptiness and existence simultaneous. The World-Honored One says this to teach practitioners that in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, at every hour of the day, in the face of circumstances and as conditions come, they should contemplate thus. Then every place is a bodhimanda, and everything increases bodhi; this is what is called the boundless-seal Dharma-gate. Again, this section is freedom from all marks in order to make clear the Thus; that is, it makes clear that all dharmas and the suchness of all dharmas are one. Because all dharmas are thus, all dharmas are Buddhadharma.

What has been said above, namely that Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas, that there is neither real nor unreal, that all is so, that all is precisely not, and that all is called, is simply to illumine the purity of the awakened nature. The pure awakened nature is utterly without form or mark. Hence the attainment of bodhi is in truth without dharma. But when form and mark are empty, that is when the awakened nature appears; hence the attainment of bodhi is likewise not unreal. Since it is neither unreal nor a real dharma, one may well make use of all dharmas to pass through affairs and train the mind, utterly emptying all marks. Why then seek to see bodhi apart from all dharmas? Why? The Heart Sutra says: all dharmas are marked with emptiness; they neither arise nor cease, are neither defiled nor pure, neither increase nor decrease. Is this not unexcelled bodhi plainly before one's eyes? In short, the self-nature is like a mani jewel that shows color according to direction, which illustrates that all dharmas are manifestations of the self-nature itself; yet within the jewel there is no color or mark at all, which illustrates that they are precisely not all dharmas. Buddhadharma is like ordinary home cooking: one should of course eat one's fill, but the eater should attend to digestion, which illustrates that one should not dwell even in bodhi. It depends on the person remaining ever awake and aware, neither clinging nor separating, and then anywhere and at any time one may obtain true benefit.

In what the Buddha teaches, when he speaks of principle he includes practice, and when he speaks of nature he includes cultivation. This whole section on every dharma being thus teaches the noble wisdom of self-realization, causing students to take it up and give rise to contemplation. One must be free from marks and free from thought before one can harmonize with it. How can it be spoken of? To speak of it at once falls into names and marks. Yet it cannot but be spoken of. Hence in explaining the practice one has no choice but to use the method of indirect hints and side remarks. Listeners must grasp it where there are no words or phrases. Everything said hereafter is like this. Keep your eyes on this.
(Chou) Fourth, the Thus in respect of the reward body.

"Subhuti, suppose a person's body were tall and large." Subhuti said, "World-Honored One, the Tathagata says that a person's body being tall and large is not a great body; therefore it is called a great body."

"Suppose a person's body were tall and large" is precisely the earlier reference in the explanation section to the simile of a person whose body is like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains. A body like Sumeru is therefore called tall and large. This refers to the Buddha's reward body. Because it was spoken of before, the elder knows its meaning well. Hence he does not wait for the sentence to be finished before making its meaning clear: it is not a great body, therefore it is called a great body. "Is called" makes clear that the mark of a tall and large body is not absent; "is not" makes clear that, since it is called tall and large, it still falls within measure and number, and should be viewed as free from marks, so that the dharma-body, being boundless, is the absolute great. The reason the elder does not wait for the sentence to be finished is to make people understand at once that this is the body like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, spoken of before. He says "the Tathagata says" precisely to make clear that the reward body and the dharma-body are one thus. At first glance this section seems to have no connection with the three sections above. In fact the meaning of those three sections becomes thoroughly clear only with this section. All that has gone before, treating of name, of the fruit of virtue, and of all dharmas in order to make clear the Thus, is spoken in terms of dharma. This section, making clear the Thus in terms of the reward body, is spoken in terms of simile; hence "suppose." The Buddha feared that those who did not understand the dharma-teaching might come to understand it through the simile. You should know that the dharma-teaching above makes clear only the principle, while this simile provides actual evidence. When the principle is confirmed by fact, it becomes all the more trustworthy and verifiable. This is why this section is placed at the end. To understand it thoroughly, one must first understand the meaning of the dharma-body and the reward body.
The dharma-body has two meanings:

(1) What is called the dharma-body is the pure self-nature. It is named the dharma-body of self-nature. This is what Buddhas and sentient beings share alike: the nature of one substance, which is also the true suchness outside of which no dharma exists. But sentient beings are within obstruction and cannot manifest it perfectly. Hence, as regards sentient beings, it is also called true suchness within obstruction, and also the dharma-body within the entanglement.

(2) All Buddhas, having cultivated myriad practices through immeasurable kalpas, adorned with merit and wisdom, cause this self-nature's light of wisdom to appear perfectly and completely. This is named the dharma-body beyond obstruction, also called true suchness beyond obstruction, and also the dharma-body attained as reward, meaning that the dharma-body, having gone beyond obstruction, is the fruition attained through the diligent cultivation of myriad practices; that is, the body of fruition. Spoken in terms of marks, it is named the reward body; hence here it says "is called a great body," meaning that "tall and large" is spoken in terms of name and mark. Spoken in terms of nature, it is the dharma-body beyond obstruction. The dharma-body is not a mark and does not fall within long or short, great or small, or number; hence here it says "is not a great body." This is enough to show that the reward body and the dharma-body are neither one nor different. (One is spoken in terms of marks and the other in terms of nature, hence not one; yet they are in fact one body, hence not different.) For this reason the reward body also has two meanings: (1) As regards its being free from all obstruction and fulfilled in pure virtue, it is called the self-reward body, that is, the dharma-body beyond obstruction and the dharma-body attained as reward, meaning that having cultivated the cause and realized the fruit, one has completed one's own salvation; hence the self-reward body. (2) As regards its pervading all circumstances and illumining everywhere, it is called the other-reward body, for the dharma-body manifests the marks attained as reward originally for the sake of others; hence the other-reward body. It can be seen that self-reward and other-reward are likewise neither one nor different. (One is spoken in terms of the benefit one receives oneself and the other in terms of causing others to receive benefit, hence not one; yet they are still one body, hence not different.) From this it is fully evident that names are all provisionally established, and equally evident that nature and mark have never been apart.

This is brought forward for no more than two purposes: to resolve doubts and to confirm the meaning. That is, to resolve the doubts of those who do not grasp the meaning, and thereby to confirm all the meanings taught above. For it guards against those who cannot harmonize what the three sections above have said and are about to doubt: since they are plainly all dharmas, why are they all Buddhadharma? Since they are one thus, why are there still all dharmas? Neither real nor unreal, what exactly does that mean? And it has been said repeatedly that in truth there is no dharma, yet the Buddha's reward body, with its radiance and excellent marks, is formed of immeasurable dharmas of merit; is that not plainly a mark of dharma? Since there is no real dharma to be attained, is the attainment of this reward body not a real dharma?

They do not realize that all dharmas are originally manifestations of the self-nature of true suchness as conditions arise. If one does not cling to the marks of dharmas, then when one sees dharmas one sees the nature of dharmas. For example, the reward body is precisely the manifest mark of the dharma-body beyond obstruction. The manifesting of marks is for the sake of others. But if one does not cling to the marks of the reward body, one sees the nature of the dharma-body, and the two do not obstruct each other. Hence although there are all dharmas, in truth they are one thus; and although they are one thus, all dharmas are no obstacle. You should know that the Tathagata's attainment of neither real nor unreal is because he has realized only the pure awakened nature in which stillness and illumination are simultaneous. For example, the reward body, though of excellent marks and radiance, does not obstruct the purity of the self-nature; indeed, because the self-nature is pure, it has excellent marks and radiance. Is this not the awakened nature's stillness and illumination simultaneous, neither real nor unreal?

Extending this to all dharmas, they are originally not real but are all provisional names. Yet knowing that they are provisional names, one knows that they are the marks of true suchness; and knowing that they are precisely not, one knows that they are all the nature of true suchness. For example, the reward body is likewise a provisional name for being tall and large; it is nothing but the light and shadow of the dharma-body of true suchness. Hence it is precisely not tall and large, and one should contemplate the pure self-nature of true suchness. For if one does not contemplate marks but contemplates nature, then the reward body is the dharma-body. Hence all dharmas are Buddhadharma. In short, when the sutra speaks of no dharma and of freedom from marks, it is to dismiss the fault of dwelling in dharmas and dwelling in marks, not to say that there is absolutely no dharma and no mark. When it speaks of no dharma to be attained, it means that one attains yet does not keep the thought of attainment, not that there is ultimately no attainment. You should know that what one should not dwell in or cling to is so because all dharmas are one thus, without unreality and without reality; it is not that there is ultimately no dharma, no mark, and no attainment, because it is precisely all dharmas that are one thus, without reality and without unreality. Once this meaning is clear, all dharmas are Buddhadharma. If this meaning is not clear, even Buddhadharma is not Buddhadharma. Hence the principle that the reward body and the dharma-body are neither one nor different must not remain unclear.

Once one understands neither one nor different, one knows that there is neither dharma nor no dharma, neither mark nor no mark, neither attainment nor no attainment; and then the suchness of all dharmas, together with neither real nor unreal and all is so, can be thoroughly understood. Why? Because they are not one, they become all dharmas and are without reality; hence "precisely not." Because they are not different, they are one thus and without unreality; hence "all is so." Knowing that within not-different one sees not-one, then although it is one thus it does not obstruct their being all dharmas. Knowing that within not-one one sees not-different, then although they are all dharmas it does not obstruct their being one thus. Moreover, when not-one, at that very moment it is not-different; and when not-different, at that very moment it is not-one. Hence neither real nor unreal. This makes clear that reality and unreality alike cannot be spoken, and so both are called no. Again, because not-one, though it is so it is called named; because not-different, though it is named it is called so. Though not-one, in fact not-different, hence it is both called named and called all is so; though not-different, in fact not-one, hence it is both called all is so and called named. In sum, though marks are not one, the nature is not different; hence all dharmas are Buddhadharma. The nature is indeed not different, yet marks remain not one; hence they are precisely not all dharmas, and are called all dharmas. Because the reward body and the dharma-body are neither one nor different is most evident, and because this principle of neither one nor different can harmonize all the meanings taught in the three sections above, the Buddha therefore finally brings up the reward body again to make them clear, so that the meaning of every dharma being thus may be utterly and perfectly manifested.

In the earlier explanation section, the reward body was brought forward to prove that one should produce the mind while dwelling nowhere. For having attained this fruit of the reward body, the Buddha still says it is not a body, it is called; this is the Buddha not dwelling in this body. Hence bodhisattvas, while cultivating the cause, should dwell nowhere; yet it is not that this surpassing and wondrous great body is absent. This body is precisely adorned by the merit and wisdom of the six paramitas and myriad practices; hence while cultivating the cause one should produce the mind of the six paramitas while dwelling nowhere. Here, however, the point is that the reward body and the dharma-body, being neither one nor different, bring about the meaning of every dharma being thus. Hence the words are the same but the intent is different.

This whole section on every dharma being thus reveals the fruit of virtue to the utmost. Revealing the fruit of virtue is for the sake of making clear the practice of the cause; hence the next section continues by making clear the cause.

(Gui) Second, making clear the cause. In two: (Zi) First, directly dismissing attachment to dharmas; second, causing the understanding of no-self. (Zi) First, again in two: (Chou) First, dismissing in terms of saving sentient beings; second, dismissing in terms of adorning lands. (Chou) First, again in two: (Yin) First, stating the dismissal; second, questioning and explaining.
(Yin) First, stating the dismissal.
"Subhuti, bodhisattvas are likewise thus. If they say, 'I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to liberation,' then they are not called bodhisattvas."

"Likewise thus" refers to the whole section above on every dharma being thus, meaning that the Buddha is the standard for bodhisattvas. Do not think that every dharma being thus is what the Buddha realized and beyond your reach. You should know that the Buddha could realize it thus because he cultivated thus in the causal ground. Hence all bodhisattvas who arouse the initial aspiration to enlightenment should likewise experience the meaning that every dharma is thus, and dwell nowhere in dharmas.

Since the two words "likewise thus" refer generally to the section above, the word thus may be taken as the oneness of all dharmas, and the word so may be taken as all is so. Taken together, they mean neither real nor unreal. All dharmas are without reality; all being one thus is without unreality. The meaning is that bodhisattvas cultivate the cause in order to attain the surpassing fruit. Since the fruit and reward body are thus, the mind of the causal ground should likewise be thus. It must correspond with the no reality of all dharmas and not grasp a single dharma; and it must also correspond with the no unreality of all being one thus and not abandon a single dharma. Moreover, when not grasping, it does not abandon; when not abandoning, it does not grasp. Thus and thus, both reality and unreality are absent. Then those who are thus in the cause will surely be thus in the fruit.

The line "bodhisattvas are likewise thus" is the general heading for both the sections on saving sentient beings and adorning lands: in both they should be thus. How does one save sentient beings? By being free from marks while practicing the six paramitas. How does one adorn lands? Also by being free from marks while practicing the six paramitas. This is what is meant by the adornment of merit and wisdom. Hence one should practice the six paramitas widely and not abandon a single dharma; and one should even more not cling to the marks of the six paramitas and not grasp a single dharma. Not abandoning and not grasping: only then does one have the qualification of a bodhisattva. Hence in both one should be thus. The words that follow, "If they say," state the opposite to make this clear: if they are not thus, they lose the qualification of a bodhisattva.

"I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to liberation" is exactly the same as the earlier words, "I should bring all sentient beings to liberation." The earlier passage says that one should produce such a mind, plainly because the World-Honored One taught it to be so. Now it says that such a one is not called a bodhisattva. Why? The implications here are deep and subtle; let me explain them in three layers:

(1) You should know that the earlier instruction to produce the mind of thus acknowledging one's full responsibility was meant to dismiss the mind that deemed itself to be bodhi. But then, having ceased to cling to bodhi, one again deems oneself to have fulfilled the responsibility. Though the face has changed, the grasping at dharmas is still the same and the dwelling in marks is still the same; discrimination and attachment remain as before. How could this be allowed? Hence the Buddha still rebukes it: such a one is not called a bodhisattva. The word "then" is closely urgent: if this thought remains in the mind even slightly, the qualification of a bodhisattva is already lost. One must contemplate with subtle and close attention, examine with subtle and close attention, enter finer and finer layer by layer, and dismiss again and again, until this mind gives rise to not a single thought and is pure without a speck of dust, so that though one liberates immeasurable beings it is as if nothing had happened. Only then does one correspond with the meaning of oneness-thus. If a single thought remains, one has already clung to marks, already grasped dharmas, already discriminated, and is still self-view.

(2) The earlier instruction not only made one know that saving sentient beings is a responsibility one ought to fulfill, thereby dismissing one's clinging to bodhi; it also made one know that this responsibility can never finally be fulfilled. As it is said, when all sentient beings have been saved, since sentient beings have no end, how could the responsibility ever be fulfilled? This dismisses the view that one is able to save. It further made one know that saving is equal to not saving, as it is said that not one sentient being has in truth been liberated. This again dismisses the view of those saved. The words of the instruction are thorough and complete. Now this man has forgotten two lines of the instruction and clings tightly to the first line alone. Is he not then smugly thinking that he can fulfill this responsibility and that he has greatly saved others? "I shall bring immeasurable beings to liberation" shows a self-congratulatory, self-important, everything-despising attitude plainly visible in the words. How could he be a bodhisattva? This fault must be sternly dismissed; hence the direct rebuke: such a one is not called a bodhisattva. There is a further deep intent in the World-Honored One's saying this: it makes those who read the sutra and hear the Dharma understand thoroughly and penetrate throughout, not holding to one point and missing ten thousand, not taking a part as the whole, not quoting out of context.

(3) This person has another serious illness: the illness of making such a statement. To say nothing of the fact that loud boastful words are improper, even if his words matched the facts, his readiness to advertise himself shows that he clings to fame and renown and that his mind is not pure. Moreover, speech is the voice of the mind; one who makes such a statement makes it because he has such a thought. If the thought has not yet ceased, he cannot even settle birth and death, and shall we call him a bodhisattva? In saying this, the World-Honored One means that those who arouse the great compassionate mind should put more effort into freedom from thought. If deluded thoughts do not cease, the true mind is forever obstructed. With compassion but no wisdom, how can one save others? And how does the thought arise? It arises because the discriminating view of self and others still remains; hence such a one is not called a bodhisattva.
(Yin) Second, questioning and explaining. In two: (Mao) First, explaining that there is no dharma; second, explaining no-self.
(Mao) First, explaining that there is no dharma.
"Why? Subhuti, there is no dharma called a bodhisattva."

The popular circulation edition reads "in truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva." The Tang dynasty manuscript sutra and the annotated editions of Master Sengzhao and Master Hui all lack the word "truly," and should be followed. Before I had seen the ancient text, I too read this sentence's meaning carelessly. When I did see the ancient text, I still thought that "in truth there is no dharma called a bodhisattva" was the same in sentence pattern as the earlier "in truth there is no dharma called an arhat," and that having the word "truly" was not unacceptable. Only after quietly pondering the meaning of the sutra before and after did I realize that the two are utterly unlike, and realize the excellence of the original text. For the earlier passage explaining that the four fruits are without thought sees the meaning only by passing through one layer. Since the questions all read, "Can he form the thought, I have attained the fruit?" the answers read, "Srotaapanna is called entering the stream, yet there is nothing entered." That is, although he is called one who has entered the stream, in his mind there is not yet anything called entering; how much less anything called a stream. Then it is clear that he has absolutely no thought of having entered the stream. The cases of Sakridagamin and Anagamin follow the same pattern, and so each is followed by "is called so-and-so," making clear that what is called stream-entry, what is called one return, and what is called non-return are all provisional names, and that such thoughts were never present at all. The meaning of arhat is "no birth," meaning that he has realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. Since not a single dharma arises, it says "in truth there is no dharma"; that is, his mind has not even a dharma, so how could there be anything called no birth? Then the one named no birth is only a provisional name; how could such a thought exist? Hence "is called an arhat." Here, however, the text makes clear why one is not called a bodhisattva: because his mind has the view that there is one who saves and one who is saved, he grasps dharmas; grasping dharmas, he clings to the marks of self, person, and the rest, and is an ordinary being. Hence that there should be a dharma called a bodhisattva is utterly impossible. There is no need to pass through one layer to make the meaning appear; hence the sentence pattern differs from the earlier one. The sentence "there is no dharma called a bodhisattva" may be read in two ways:

(1) Pause briefly at the word "no," and read the following six words in one breath. The meaning is: why is he not called a bodhisattva? The sutra answers in the negative to explain: that there is a dharma called a bodhisattva is not something the Buddha ever said. Hence the text immediately continues: therefore the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, person, being, or life. This makes clear that where there is a dharma one clings to self and person, discriminates, contradicts the Buddha's teaching, and is an ordinary being. Thus there is no such thing as a dharma called a bodhisattva. For this section's "there is no dharma called a bodhisattva" explains the reason why the section above says one is not called a bodhisattva; and the next section's "dharmas are without self" explains the reason why this section says there is no dharma called a bodhisattva. This is what is meant by explaining and completing in turn.

(2) Read the seven words as one sentence. As the Tang dynasty Master Guifeng says in his commentary: "If there is no dharma called a bodhisattva, how could there be an 'I' saving sentient beings?" That is, if there is not even a dharma called a bodhisattva, how could there be the mark of an I saving sentient beings? The intent is to show that the words above, "I shall save sentient beings," are a grasping at the dharma of saving sentient beings as the way to become a bodhisattva. Master Sengzhao of the Jin dynasty comments: "The bodhisattva is himself absent; how could there be sentient beings?" "Himself absent" means not even present. The meaning is that bodhisattva and sentient beings are both provisional names: if there is not even a bodhisattva who saves, how could there be sentient beings who are saved? Then it is clear that one should not grasp at saving sentient beings. Looking at the intent of this commentary, the word dharma is seen even more flexibly, as much as to say that there is no way to be called a bodhisattva. In short, the ancient commentaries mostly clarify the great meaning and do not fuss over the tone and flow of words before and after. Hence in reading the ancient commentaries one should also let go of the outward appearance and take the spirit, being good at comprehending.
(Mao) Second, explaining no-self.
"Therefore the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without person, without being, and without life."

"Therefore" connects what precedes and introduces what follows. Wishing to explain the reason why there is no dharma called a bodhisattva, the text sets forth the principle that the Buddha teaches all dharmas to be without self. The Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, person, being, or life. You should know that the views of sentient beings are nothing but discrimination. Where there is discrimination there is the opposition of subject and object. As regards the seeing subject, it is self; as regards the seen object, it is person; the views of subject and object give rise to a profusion of differences, and this is being. This is spoken horizontally. When the views of subject and object continue without interruption, this is life. This is spoken vertically.

The deluded mind of discrimination is too numerous to count. Taken horizontally and vertically through subject and object, nothing is left out. This is why this sutra, among all kinds of views and all kinds of marks, singles out these four to speak of. Yet discrimination arises from clinging to self; hence it is opened into four, while taken together it is simply one self-view. They do not realize that all dharmas are originally without self and without difference.
This line, "the Buddha says," contains a great deal; it should be taken in two readings to make it clear:

(1) Pause at the word "says." It means that the principle that all dharmas are without self is what the Buddha taught. All dharmas arise only when conditions meet, and arising is itself non-arising. For what is called arising is nothing but the illusory mark of conditions meeting; how could there be a real dharma? Hence arising is itself non-arising. This the Buddha constantly taught. If arising is itself non-arising, how could there be self or person, or difference? You should know that wherever there is self and person and difference, the fault lies in the ordinary being's grasping. Within all dharmas, how could such a thing exist? Hence it was said above: if the mind grasps at marks, then it clings to self, person, being, and life. If it does not grasp, then there is neither subject nor object, and not a single mark arises. How then can a bodhisattva say, "I shall bring sentient beings to liberation"? That is to grasp at the dharma of the six paramitas, and then self and person stand opposed and the four marks are plainly there. This is an ordinary being; how could he be called a bodhisattva? Hence that there should be a dharma called a bodhisattva is utterly impossible.

(2) Pause at the word "dharmas." It means that all the dharmas the Buddha taught are originally without difference of self and person. Here two meanings should be set out. (A) Whatever the Buddha taught, he taught what he had realized; and what the Buddha realized is nothing but the oneness of all dharmas. Hence all the dharmas the Buddha taught are nothing but means to cause people to obliterate the marks of dharmas in opposition and discrimination, and to awaken to the nature of dharmas in equal oneness. To awaken to this awakened nature is what may be called a bodhisattva. If one keeps a mark of dharma, that is attachment to self, that is opposition, that is discrimination; how could it be called awakening? Hence that there should be a dharma called a bodhisattva was never the Buddha's meaning at all. (B) All the dharmas the Buddha taught are meant to cause hearers to be without self of person, without self of dharmas, and to eliminate the discriminating mind. For the one true dharma-realm is originally without the differences of self and person; it is with such differences that one becomes a sentient being. The Buddha teaches the Dharma in order to save sentient beings. Hence all dharmas are nothing but the meaning of the one true dharma-realm, meant to cause the elimination of self-attachment. Therefore not a single dharma should be grasped, for grasping is to cling to self, person, being, and life. A bodhisattva is one who learns from the Buddha. If he grasps at the dharmas of the six paramitas and the rest, how can he be called one who learns from the Buddha? Why? Because that there should be a dharma called a bodhisattva is not what the Buddha taught. (Here it does not say "the Tathagata says" but "the Buddha says," precisely to reveal the principle that cause and fruit are one thus. Buddha is the fruit-person; bodhisattva is the cause-person. Since the fruit-person speaks thus, the cause-person should learn thus.) In short, all sentient beings are by nature of one substance, originally without the division of you and me in opposition. Hence when we speak of sentient beings, the bodhisattva is also a sentient being; and when we speak of the bodhisattva, sentient beings are also bodhisattvas. Sentient beings are originally Buddhas, how much more so a bodhisattva?

Moreover, beings are originally unborn; what is there to save? And saving is also self-saving; how can it be called saving beings? For example, when the head is on fire, the hand must save it; even the most foolish would not fail to save it. Yet there is decidedly no discrimination of a savior and a saved, because one knows that the savior is precisely the saved and the saved is precisely the savior. The bodhisattva and all sentient beings are likewise thus. Hence the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, person, being, or life, so that hearers may contemplate the nature of one substance. If one says, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to liberation," is that not the view of self, the view of person, the view of being? If this view is not removed for a single day, is that not the view of life? With such discrimination and such attachment, one is wholly estranged from the meaning that the nature is of one substance and all dharmas are one thus, and plainly contradicts the Buddha's teaching; and one still considers oneself a bodhisattva? One says one shall save immeasurable beings, yet I fear one cannot save even three or five. Why? Because once I am I and sentient beings are sentient beings, then when meeting those who accept one's saving, one is sure to be self-congratulatory and pleased; when meeting those who do not accept it, one is sure to slight and resent them; and when meeting others who practice the six paramitas, one is sure to contend and grow suspicious. Emotional clinging turns round and round, and one binds and entangles oneself. You yourself are walking into a dense forest of affliction and evil views, and still you speak of saving sentient beings, still you would be called a bodhisattva? Hence that there should be a dharma called a bodhisattva is utterly impossible in reason and in fact. All who arouse the right awakening must earnestly experience the principle that the Buddha's teaching that all dharmas are without self, person, being, or life is precisely the oneness of all dharmas. Though they practice the six paramitas widely, they do not grasp a single dharma. Only then is the mind empty of deluded thoughts and so without reality, and the merit not in vain and so without unreality.

This section on no-self both concludes the text above and introduces the text below. For the next section, "is not adornment, is called adornment," also teaches the meaning that the nature of dharmas is without difference, and is continuous with the meaning taught in this section.
(Chou) Second, dismissing in terms of adorning lands. In two: (Yin) First, stating the dismissal; second, questioning and explaining.
"Subhuti, if a bodhisattva says, 'I shall adorn the Buddha-lands,' such a one is not called a bodhisattva."

A bodhisattva's cultivation of the six paramitas is nothing but seeking above and transforming below. Above, the text has already made clear transforming below in terms of saving sentient beings; hence this section again makes clear seeking above in terms of adorning lands. Seeking above means seeking the way of enlightenment above. Yet seeking the way of enlightenment above is also for the sake of transforming sentient beings below, for a bodhisattva's arousing of the mind is solely for the benefit of sentient beings. The fault spoken of here is likewise the same as in the case of saving sentient beings: the fault lies in making the statement "I shall." All the various errors spoken of in the section above apply here as well, and need not be repeated. In short, to make a statement is to move thought; "I shall" is to cling to a view. To give rise to thought and cling to views like this is wholly the ordinary emotional mind; how could one be called a bodhisattva? Hence it says that such a one is not called a bodhisattva.
(Yin) Second, questioning and explaining.
"Why? The Tathagata says: what is called adorning the Buddha-lands is not adornment; therefore it is called adornment."

"Why?" asks the reason why such a one is not called a bodhisattva. "Is not" and "is called" are still as explained before: not clinging to marks and returning to nature. These two statements alone make the reason why such a one is not called a bodhisattva quite clear. For because he clings to marks and is blind to nature, he is not called a bodhisattva.

The adorning of Buddha-lands has been spoken of before, but the meaning made clear here differs from before. The difference lies in the three words "the Tathagata says." "The Tathagata says" makes clear that he speaks in terms of nature, and that then all dharmas are one thus, and one should not keep the slightest emotional view of discrimination and attachment. The earlier mention of this was to reveal the meaning that one should produce the mind while dwelling nowhere, so that one might know that when not grasping one does not abandon. The present mention of it is to make clear the meaning that one should produce the mind yet dwell nowhere. (It was said above: one should produce such a mind. Now these two sections on saving sentient beings and adorning lands teach that although one should produce such a mind, one should also not dwell in it.) This is so that one may know that when not abandoning one does not grasp. For the earlier passage caused those who arouse the bodhisattva mind to be free from marks while cultivating merit and wisdom; the present passage causes those who practice the bodhisattva path, while cultivating merit and wisdom, not to keep the view that this is merit and wisdom. The depth of the earlier and later passages differs greatly. You should know that the Buddha is the mind (as it is said, this mind is the Buddha) and that a land is the ground; a Buddha-land is as much as to say the ground of the mind. What is called adornment is this: because sentient beings from beginningless time have had this pure mind obstructed on every side by all defiled dharmas, so that what was originally empty and still is wholly disturbed, and what was originally luminous is wholly darkened, the Buddha therefore causes them to arouse vast vows to expand their measure, and to cultivate the six paramitas to remove their selfishness, being free from marks and free from thought, and to sweep away and scrub clean all the ordinary emotions and worldly views of discrimination and attachment. It is like sweeping away the obstructive things and filthy stains on the ground, to restore the original aspect of emptiness, stillness, and luminosity. There is no way to name it, so it is named adornment. In truth there is no such thing as adornment. To declare, "I shall adorn," and set this one view across the mind-ground, makes it not empty and not still, and obstructs its luminosity; can that be called adornment? One has no comprehension whatever of the essence of nature and contradicts what the Tathagata says; hence such a one is not called a bodhisattva. One must deeply understand the purport of "is not" and "is called," be free from marks and return to nature, one thus and unmoved. Then though one adorns fervently, one forgets that it is adornment, and one may come to correspond with the nature that is empty and still. Being both empty and still, luminosity appears of itself. Adorning the Buddha-lands is thus, thus; let bodhisattvas understand this!

To save sentient beings widely (the text above says "bring immeasurable beings to liberation," which is the meaning of widely) is great compassion. To purify the mind-ground (adorning Buddha-lands, spoken thoroughly, is precisely purifying the mind-ground) is great wisdom. Great compassion and great wisdom are what is called unexcelled bodhi. Putting together the meanings taught in these two sections on saving sentient beings and adorning lands, they make clear that one who arouses bodhi must not keep the thought that this is great compassion and great wisdom. If one keeps this thought even slightly, it is attachment to dharmas and is not bodhi. The two statements that such a one is not called a bodhisattva precisely complete the meaning stated when the chapter opened: in truth there is no dharma by which one arouses anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. The structure is extremely tight and the meaning extremely complete.
(Zi) Second, causing the understanding of no-self. In two: (Chou) First, marking out and indicating the understanding; second, opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision.
(Chou) First, marking out and indicating the understanding.
"Subhuti, if a bodhisattva understands the dharma of no-self, the Tathagata names him a true bodhisattva."

This section's text has always been taken as concluding the above. Yet if one traces the flow of the words carefully, the earlier statement that the Buddha teaches all dharmas to be without self reveals the meaning that the nature of dharmas is without difference, and so concludes that in saving sentient beings one should not grasp dharmas; and the statement above that "is not adornment, is called adornment" likewise reveals the meaning that the nature of dharmas is without difference, and so concludes that in adorning lands one should not grasp dharmas. Since the nature of dharmas is without difference, not a single dharma should be dwelt in; and then the meaning that in truth there is no dharma by which one arouses bodhi is completed as well. There is no need to conclude again. Moreover, if one savors the later text carefully, one knows that the earlier mention that the Buddha teaches all dharmas to be without self serves as a lead-in for this section's causing the understanding of the dharma of no-self. And when the text reaches the fourth great section later, the section on proof, it says that knowing all dharmas to be without self, one attains patient acceptance; this concludes this section. Now, about to open and reveal the Buddha's knowledge and vision and cause its understanding, the Buddha first sets down this section, "if a bodhisattva understands the dharma of no-self," as a marker. The structure is orderly and runs through in one breath. Hence if one judges this section to be a marker, what precedes and follows is harmonious. If one merely takes it as concluding the above, then the flow of energy is not linked and the spirit does not gather.

The dharma of no-self is the same as no-self of dharmas, but there is a distinction. To realize the oneness of all dharmas is called no-self of dharmas; to understand all dharmas as the oneness-thus is called the dharma of no-self. Thus the passage above in which the Buddha teaches all dharmas to be without self is because the Buddha has already realized the principle of no-self and possesses the wisdom of no-self, being able to be without self within all dharmas; hence it is called no-self of dharmas. The concluding passage later says that knowing all dharmas to be without self, one attains patient acceptance; this makes clear that one not only can know all dharmas to be without self but is also patiently at peace in no-self; hence it is likewise called no-self of dharmas. Here the point is to cause the understanding of all dharmas as originally without self; hence it is called the dharma of no-self.

You should know that the fault of attachment to dharmas lies in being obstructed by self-view. Within all dharmas, where is there ever a self?
