The present causing of understanding is to cause the removal of the obstruction. Once the obstruction of self-view is removed, one realizes the nature of dharmas that is originally without self. Hence the words "understanding the dharma of no-self" are as much as to say eliminating the deluded mind of discrimination and seeing the true nature that is originally without discrimination. In short, all dharmas are without self, and so all are the dharma of no-self. Hence from putting on the robe and carrying the bowl, entering the city to beg, and returning to one's place and sitting down, all is a demonstration of the dharma of no-self. Why? The World-Honored One himself had no need of food and clothing; it was for the sake of sentient beings that for three hundred and sixty days a year, and indeed for forty-nine years, he mingled among the toils of the dust. Had he not been utterly without self, forgetting that he was the Buddha, could he have done so? This is precisely the atmosphere of all dharmas being one thus and all dharmas being Buddhadharma; and it is precisely the concrete, solid evidence of the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata attained, in which there is neither the real nor the unreal. This is why the elder Subhuti rose from his seat in the assembly and, bowing in homage, praised him: "Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Tathagata skillfully protects and instructs all bodhisattvas." Because the Tathagata day after day mingles among the toils of the dust and does not leave sentient beings, it is said that he skillfully protects; and because he simply passes his days as conditions come, forgetting the dharma of self, and day after day thus practices the teaching without words, it is said that he skillfully instructs. Alas that the elder alone could understand it well, while the rest of the assembly remained dimly unaware! Hence the elder had no choice but to request the teaching in detail. And from the point where he asked how bodhisattvas should subdue their minds, going layer by layer up to the section above, all of it was meant to break attachment to self. Then whatever is taught is without exception the dharma of no-self, and all of it should be understood.

Does the present phrase "understanding the dharma of no-self" then refer to what has been said above, or is there a separate dharma of no-self? You should know that there is no separate dharma, and that there is no separate absence of dharma. Why? Because all dharmas are without self. One must not say that only what has been said above is right and everything else is wrong. If one can understand it well, then one need not wait for the World-Honored One to open his mouth: while passing the days as conditions come, dressing and eating, one has long since understood it thoroughly. It is only because people cannot that all the dharmas above were spoken of. And our World-Honored One, in his great compassion and great mercy, pitying all sentient beings and fearing that even having heard all these dharmas they may still not understand, is about to teach the fundamental skillful means that will bring understanding. Hence at this point, continuing from the Buddha's teaching that all dharmas are without self, he specially marks it out: "If a bodhisattva understands the dharma of no-self, the Tathagata names him a true bodhisattva." This is to make the assembly rouse their spirits and listen attentively to what follows, so that they will not treat it as commonplace and carelessly let it pass.

What is the fundamental skillful means? It is the opening of the Buddha's knowledge and vision that follows. All students of Buddhism know the harm of self-view, yet because the root of the illness is too deep they cannot remove it. Though they plainly study the dharma of no-self, they still cling to their old ways and cling to self everywhere. What then is to be done? There is nothing for it but to instill the Buddha's knowledge and vision with all one's strength, so as to transform one's old ordinary emotions and worldly views, and thus come to understand all the dharma of no-self taught before and after. From this it may be said that opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision is in particular the wondrous dharma for no-self. (It can be seen that the meaning made clear in the opening of the Buddha's knowledge and vision holds an especially important place in the whole sutra, and that its meaning must first be thoroughly understood.) And yet dharma is precisely not dharma. If, hearing of opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision, one keeps a knowledge and vision, that again becomes attachment to dharmas and again is self-view. How could that be the Buddha's knowledge and the Buddha's vision? This principle should be pondered long and deeply. To understand means to be unobstructed on every side, without any blockage. (Understanding is what is called opening.) Sentient beings, in the face of all dharmas, are moved to obstruction and cannot understand, because of partial clinging. Partial clinging is self-view. Now the text causes them to open the Buddha's perfect vision; being perfect, they do not cling. It causes them to open the Buddha's right knowledge; being right, they are not partial. Hence one who would open the wisdom of no-self and reach the essential principle of no-self must first understand his knowledge and vision, so that seeing may be wholly perfect and knowing wholly right. Is this not the fundamental skillful means? In sum, it makes clear that in advancing in practice the first thing is to open understanding and remove partial clinging.

"The Tathagata names him a true bodhisattva": if one understands the dharma of no-self, then one understands the oneness of all dharmas; hence it says "the Tathagata says" and says "true." Yet the essence of nature is empty and still; how could there be the name and mark of a bodhisattva? Hence it says "names." This makes known that what is called a true bodhisattva is likewise a provisional name in speech, and must not be clung to either. To cling is again not empty and still, and not one thus.

The dharma of no-self may also be divided into no-self and no-dharma. Yet whether it be no-self of persons or no-self of dharmas, it is always one attachment to self. The no-self of dharmas is subtler than the no-self of persons; when the self of dharmas is absent, the self of persons is absent of itself. Hence there is no need to divide it rigidly into two.

blocks.text: One Body, One Contemplation, Part Eighteen

inline.s: (Chou) Second, opening the Buddha's knowledge and vision. In two: (Yin) First, making clear the perfect vision; second, making clear the right knowledge. (Yin) First, again in two: (Mao) First, making clear non-attachment to the one; second, making clear non-attachment to the different.
(Mao) First, making clear non-attachment to the one.

"Subhuti, what do you think? Does the Tathagata have the flesh eye?" "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathagata has the flesh eye." "Subhuti, what do you think? Does the Tathagata have the divine eye?" "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathagata has the divine eye." "Subhuti, what do you think? Does the Tathagata have the wisdom eye?" "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathagata has the wisdom eye." "Subhuti, what do you think? Does the Tathagata have the dharma eye?" "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathagata has the dharma eye." "Subhuti, what do you think? Does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye?" "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathagata has the Buddha eye."

This "vision" is not confined to what the eye sees; it is as much as to say one's outlook. Knowledge and vision both issue from principle and wisdom and are originally not different entities. (Principle means the essence of principle, that is, the self-nature. Principle-wisdom means the wisdom inherent in the nature, making clear that it does not come from outside.) Yet spoken in terms of what is manifested outwardly, it is called vision; spoken in terms of what is clearly understood within, it is called knowledge. Hence one cannot force a division into two, nor can one definitively say they are one. Moreover, knowledge and vision support each other: when one knows deeply, one's outlook is naturally not shallow. Yet if one does not break one's old views, one cannot open new knowledge either. Hence in the text vision is spoken of first and knowledge afterward.
Let me first speak of the names and marks of the five eyes, and then make clear the purport of the Buddha's teaching the five eyes.

The flesh eye is the eye that belongs to this body of blood and flesh. The supreme-meaning pure faculty, relying on the physical body, has that whereby it illumines and sees; this is named the flesh eye. What this eye sees is limited: it can see only forms within an obstruction (as opposed to beyond an obstruction). The supreme-meaning pure faculty is another name for the pure seeing nature. That what it sees is limited is because it is obstructed by affliction.

The divine eye may be obtained through the power of karma, as the heavens of desire obtain it through the karma of merit; or it may be obtained through the power of concentration, as in the form heavens and the formless heavens, all of which are by the power of concentration. The power of concentration means cultivating visualization, visualizing objects beyond an obstruction. (Beyond an obstruction is said in contrast with what the flesh eye sees, which is within an obstruction.) When the visualization is accomplished, one sees matters beyond the obstruction, that is, matters the flesh eye cannot see. This is named the divine eye. One need not necessarily be born in heaven: even in the human realm, one who obtains this power of concentration can have it. This refers to those who specially cultivate this concentration. As for the divine eye of one born in the heavens of desire, it is obtained by cultivating the karma of merit; and the divine eye of one born in the form heavens and above, whether obtained by cultivating other kinds of concentration, is in every case obtained as reward. Ordinary beings reach only as far as these two eyes. As for the wisdom eye and above, one cannot have them without cultivating world-transcending dharmas.

The wisdom eye illumines and sees the principle of true emptiness by means of fundamental wisdom. (This is also called ultimate truth.) Wisdom is itself insight, hence the wisdom eye. Fundamental wisdom has many other names: wisdom in accordance with reality, true wisdom, wisdom of the essential substance, wisdom in accordance with principle, and so on. Because it can give rise to subsequently attained wisdom, it is called fundamental wisdom. The sages and worthies of the Two Vehicles reach only as far as this. Having it, one also has the divine eye, and surpasses the divine eye, being able to see what the divine eye cannot see. Yet it too has limits and does not come up to the Buddha's wisdom eye.

The dharma eye illumines and sees the matters of difference by means of subsequently attained wisdom. (That is, conventional truth.) It too has many other names, such as provisional wisdom, conventional wisdom, all-pervading wisdom, wisdom in accordance with measure, and so on. Because it can be obtained only after obtaining fundamental wisdom, it is called subsequently attained wisdom. One who obtains this wisdom not only realizes the principle of true emptiness and understands all Buddhadharma but also understands all worldly dharmas and all the differentiated matters of sentient beings' causes and effects, their arising of thoughts, and so on; hence the dharma eye. Yet it still does not come up to the Buddha's dharma eye. Bodhisattvas reach only as far as this. The first three eyes are all present in bodhisattvas, needless to say; they simply lack the Buddha eye.

The Buddha eye is such that wisdom is nowhere not ultimate and illumination nowhere not perfect. Only the Buddha has it; hence the Buddha eye. An ancient worthy has a verse: "The divine eye penetrates without obstruction; the flesh eye is obstructed and does not penetrate. The dharma eye can observe the conventional; the wisdom eye illumines true emptiness. The Buddha eye is like a thousand suns: it illumines differences, yet its essence remains the same." "It illumines differences, yet its essence remains the same" means that it is only in terms of the surpassing excellence of its illumination that it is named the Buddha eye; in fact its essence is not something apart from the first four. Hence as regards the first four when spoken of from the Buddha's side, though one is named the flesh eye, it sees countless worlds, unlike an ordinary being's flesh eye, which is limited and sees only within an obstruction. As for the divine eye, an ordinary being's divine eye sees only what the flesh eye cannot see; the divine eye of the Two Vehicles sees only one trichiliocosm; the divine eye of bodhisattvas, though surpassing the Two Vehicles, does not come up to the Buddha's. Only the Tathagata's divine eye can see Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. As for the wisdom eye, that of the Two Vehicles can illumine only the emptiness of self; the wisdom eye of bodhisattvas on the grounds also partially realizes the emptiness of dharmas; the Buddha's wisdom eye perfectly illumines the three emptinesses and penetrates the true nature. As for the dharma eye, that of bodhisattvas, since the obstruction of the knowable is not yet exhausted, has its own limits on each ground; only the Buddha's dharma eye, with the obstruction of the knowable exhausted, knows all dharmas, and so liberates every being born. From this one may know that spoken from the Buddha's side, they are merely named four eyes, expressing that he responds as soon as anything moves him; in fact there is only the one Buddha eye. Hence the ancient worthy said that the first four, in the Buddha, are all named the Buddha eye.

That the Buddha eye is such that wisdom is nowhere not ultimate and illumination nowhere not perfect: spoken in terms of conventional truth, it knows and sees the number of raindrops in worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges; other things may be imagined. Hence from beginningless time to the end of the future, throughout space and to the limits of the dharma-realm, it knows and sees without exception every sentient being, even the most minute, dying here and being born there, their faculties and natures and families, and all the infinitely varied and most minute matters of their arising of thoughts and their causes and effects. Spoken in terms of ultimate truth, the hearers have much concentration and little wisdom, and so illumine only the emptiness of self and do not see the Buddha-nature. Bodhisattvas have much wisdom and little concentration; though they see the Buddha-nature, they do not yet see it fully. For the realization of the Buddha-nature takes wisdom as its direct cause and concentration as its indirect condition; the cause being near and the condition far, much concentration does not come up to much wisdom. Yet since concentration and wisdom are not yet equal, bodhisattvas only partially realize the emptiness of dharmas and partially see the Buddha-nature. Only Buddha and Buddha, with concentration and wisdom equal, see the nature clearly, as one sees an amalaka fruit in the palm of the hand. Here ends the explanation of the names and marks.

What is the purport of the Buddha's teaching the five eyes? It is to make clear, by means of the five eyes, that the Buddha's vision is perfectly fused. The text of this section is most extraordinary: it rises suddenly and stops abruptly. It sets out the five eyes in plain order and adds not a word besides, so its meaning is very hard to grasp. One must read it together with the section above to know that it is meant to cause the understanding of the Buddha's vision. The word "know" in the text below is meant to cause the opening of the Buddha's knowledge. This is why the section above must be judged to be a general marker.

To bring up one Buddha eye is to include the four eyes. Yet here the text brings up each of the four eyes in turn and asks, and each is answered "has." This precisely makes clear non-attachment to any one vision. If all four eyes were answered "does not have" and only the Buddha eye answered "has," that would be clinging exclusively to one Buddha eye; how could that be the Buddha's perfect vision, how could it be no-self of dharmas? The elder deeply understood the purport and understood the dharma of no-self, and so did not answer thus. Spoken from the Buddha's side, the flesh eye, divine eye, wisdom eye, and dharma eye are each surpassing, and these four eyes together are the Buddha eye. Then the text further brings up the Buddha eye and asks, and it too is answered "has." This precisely makes clear that apart from the four eyes there is no separate Buddha eye, apart from the Buddha eye no separate four eyes, and apart from each single eye no separate single eye. Yet as he responds to whatever moves him, what harm is there in there being each single eye? In bringing up all five eyes, the intent is to make clear that they are not one yet one, one yet not one; that every vision is perfect, and there is no such thing as one vision being not one vision. Then to call it seeing yet not seeing is acceptable; to call it not seeing yet seeing is also acceptable; and to call it not existing yet existing, existing yet not existing, is acceptable as well. This is the utmost of non-attachment to the one. Hence the answers all first say "yes" and then say "has." For it makes clear that once one sees the oneness-thus, then whatever is seen is so. Why? Because vision is thus.

That both question and answer say the Tathagata has them is simply to make clear that the seeing nature is perfect and luminous, like a perfect mirror: when a foreigner comes, a foreigner appears; when a Chinese comes, a Chinese appears, with no partiality at all. This is precisely what is meant by not existing yet existing, existing yet not existing. For example, divide one pool into five pools, and each pool shows the moon. The moon becomes five along with the pools, yet the moon has no partiality: this is one yet not one. If the five pools are joined into one pool, then one moon appears. The moon becomes one along with the pool, and the moon likewise has no partiality: this is not one yet one. The Buddha eye and the five eyes are thus, thus. This precisely reveals the meaning that all dharmas are without self. Bodhisattvas should open such vision and understand such a dharma of no-self. How does one understand it? Only by not clinging to one's own views, and further not clinging to any single view. How can one not cling? First of all one should greatly open one's perfect understanding, so that one's outlook becomes thorough, and then the clinging mind thins of itself. Then one should further exert effort to eliminate habit, be free from marks and free from thought, and realize the oneness of all dharmas; only then is it ultimate.

"What do you think?" probes how deep his outlook is. Each answer, "Yes, the Tathagata has," is enough to prove that the elder has already understood the principle of oneness-thus without obstruction. Wherever the sutra says "what do you think," it is always a phrase probing one's outlook. Wherever it says "if one forms the thought," "can one form the thought," "do not form the thought," "do not say that one forms the thought," and so on, it is always breaking a clinging view and causing the opening of perfect vision.
(Mao) Second, making clear non-attachment to the different.
"Subhuti, what do you think? As for all the sands in the Ganges, does the Buddha say they are sands?" "Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathagata says they are sands."

In the popular circulation edition the words "as for" are followed by "thus," which the ancient text does not have. The ancient text should be followed. Because of this one word "thus," many take the passage to be speaking a simile, merely to lead into what follows, and do not realize that it is speaking the literal truth. They do not realize that in teaching this section, together with all the sections above, the Buddha is making clear a vital meaning of Mahayana Buddhadharma, which is precisely the Buddha's perfect vision. What is called opening the Buddha's vision is the opening of this. Because of the mistaken reading, the whole thing has been blotted out at once. A single word's difference makes an immeasurable divergence; how lamentable!

The two lines, "Yes, World-Honored One," are the elder's answer. The sands of the river are minute, like motes of dust. The text above says: as for all motes of dust, the Tathagata says they are not motes of dust, therefore they are called motes of dust. Then the Tathagata must also say that the sands of the Ganges are not sands, and are therefore called sands. Why? This sutra dismisses marks, and even says that prajñā is not prajñā, to say nothing of sands. Yet here it is not so: the Tathagata says they are sands. For if one does not cling to marks, then to see marks is to see the nature; why need one say they are not sands? This is one meaning. Again, the second half of the sutra precisely makes clear that all is so, in order to dismiss the subtlest clinging (that is, the innate twofold attachment to self and dharmas). Hence even in the trivial matter of sands, it does not say "not" but only says "are." This is another meaning. Yet the point of the Buddha's teaching this section, together with the whole section on the five eyes above, to make clear a vital meaning of the Mahayana, does not lie even here.

You should know that the meaning of this section is to reveal that the Buddha eye, because it penetrates all the differentiated matters of dharmas, does not destroy conventional truth. Hence since the world says they are sands, the Tathagata also says they are sands in accord with the world, making clear that the Tathagata does not cling to different views. The elder's mind and the Buddha's mind are sealed in mutual accord; hence he answers "Yes." Since one has realized the oneness of all dharmas, whatever one says must be right; hence it says that the Tathagata says they are sands.

That the Tathagata says they are sands makes clear that the words "they are sands" are spoken by the Tathagata; that is, they are spoken in accordance with thus, and are certainly not the same as an ordinary being's saying. Why? When an ordinary being says they are sands, he grasps them as real. When the Tathagata says they are sands, it is precisely not-sands yet sands, sands yet not-sands. This is why he does not cling to different views and yet says they are sands. (Wherever the sutra says "thus," it contains this meaning; one may quietly ponder it.)

These two sections on non-attachment to the one and non-attachment to the different contain meanings profound and subtle, and must be peeled away layer by layer. For if this vision is not opened, the clinging mind is hard to dismiss. One should urgently investigate and penetrate them, so as to understand them thoroughly. They must on no account be neglected.

You should know that the meaning of not-one and not-different is precisely every dharma being thus, and this is exactly what the Buddha realized and attained. Earlier, when speaking of every dharma being thus, this was already discussed at length. Since it is the Buddha's own realization, it is the Buddha's perfect vision. Yet the Buddha realized it thus because even in the causal ground he was already able to open this perfect vision. Only by opening this perfect vision could he, though seeing, not establish a view; could he be unattached to all dharmas and so without self; and could he realize it thus, thus, perfectly. Therefore all bodhisattvas, in the causal ground of cultivation, should likewise open it. Why? Because non-attachment to the one and the different is the sword of wisdom that breaks self-view.

You should know that self-view is hard to remove for no more than two reasons: first, one's understanding of principle is unclear; second, one is self-righteous. At first, because the understanding of principle is unclear, one becomes self-righteous; afterward, because one is self-righteous, the understanding becomes even less clear. The two in fact support and increase each other. Yet their root of illness is simply the one unclear understanding of principle; self-righteousness is produced by that unclarity, and their mutual increase is a later development. Hence to break the self, one must first clarify principle. To open the Buddha's perfect vision is to clarify principle thoroughly. The five eyes are spoken of first to make clear non-attachment to one view: this is spoken for the sake of those whose understanding of principle is unclear. The Ganges sands are then spoken of to make clear non-attachment to different views: this is spoken for the sake of those who are self-righteous.
